why: Least privilege means each tier accepts traffic only from the tier directly in front of it. Security groups can reference other security groups, so the web server group allows 443 only from the load balancer's security group and the MySQL group allows 3306 only from the web server security group.

others.A: Allowing 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 on private web servers grants far more access than needed, since only the load balancer must reach them.
others.B: Network ACLs are attached to subnets, cannot reference security groups, and opening 443 to 0.0.0.0/0 is not least privilege.
others.D: Network ACLs are stateless subnet-level controls that cannot use a security group as a source, so the 3306 rule as written is impossible.

tip: Chain security groups by referencing the upstream tier's security group ID instead of CIDR ranges.

why: Repeated identical queries are the textbook case for an in-memory cache. Amazon ElastiCache (Redis or Memcached) lets the backend serve those datasets from memory with sub-millisecond latency, offloading the RDS instance and fixing the slowdown.

others.A: Amazon SNS is a pub/sub messaging service and cannot store or cache query results.
others.C: A read replica offloads reads but still executes each query against disk-backed storage; it is not a cache and adds replication lag.
others.D: Kinesis Data Firehose delivers streaming data to destinations and does nothing to speed up database reads.

tip: Frequent identical reads = ElastiCache; read scaling for varied queries = read replicas.

why: Least privilege means giving the engineer only what CloudFormation work requires. An IAM user in a group whose policy allows only CloudFormation actions limits the human's own permissions, and an IAM role scoped to the stack's resources (a CloudFormation service role) lets stacks create resources without giving the user broad direct access.

others.A: Root user credentials have unrestricted access and should never be used for daily tasks.
others.B: PowerUserAccess grants full access to almost all services, far beyond what CloudFormation operations need.
others.C: AdministratorAccess grants full access to everything and violates least privilege.

tip: Use a CloudFormation service role so users need only cloudformation:* and iam:PassRole, not every resource permission.

why: Default network ACLs allow all traffic, and the default VPC route table already includes a local route between all subnets. What blocks the connection is the RDS security group, which by default allows no inbound traffic from the web tier, so an inbound rule on port 3306 referencing the web tier's security group fixes it.

others.A: The default network ACL already allows all inbound and outbound traffic, so no extra ACL rule is needed.
others.B: The local route for the VPC CIDR already exists in every route table, so subnets can already route to each other.
others.C: Splitting into two VPCs with peering adds complexity and still would not fix the security group that is blocking traffic.

tip: Default NACL = allow all; default local route = intra-VPC reachability; custom SG = deny all inbound until you add rules.

why: RDS read replicas use asynchronous replication to give a separate, readable copy of the database. Pointing reporting queries at a read replica isolates that read load from the primary, so write performance on production is not affected.

others.B: Elastic Load Balancers do not distribute database connections across RDS instances, and RDS cannot be scaled out for writes this way.
others.C: A bigger instance still serves both workloads on the same database, so heavy reports can still hurt writes, and it costs more.
others.D: In a standard Multi-AZ instance deployment the standby cannot serve reads; it exists only for failover.

tip: Multi-AZ = availability; read replicas = read scaling.

why: The key pairs sticky sessions on the ALB, which keeps a user on the same instance during a transaction, with an ElastiCache for Redis cluster as a shared external session store. Redis supports replication, Multi-AZ failover and persistence (AOF/RDB), so session state survives an instance failing or being scaled in.

others.B: DynamoDB is a durable, serverless session store and is arguably the better fit for the durability requirement, but the keyed pairing uses Redis instead.
others.C: Amazon Cognito user pools handle authentication and tokens, not application session or cart state.
others.E: Systems Manager Application Manager is an operations console for managing applications, not a session store.

tip: External session stores (ElastiCache or DynamoDB) make web tiers stateless; sticky sessions alone are not durable.
flag: Votes are split, and 'store session data durably' points more to DynamoDB (B) than in-memory Redis (D), so A+B is arguably a better answer than A+D.

why: The web tier is stateless and needs no local storage, so the only backups it needs are current AMIs to relaunch instances through Auto Scaling. RDS automated backups with point-in-time recovery (restore to any second within the retention window, typically within about 5 minutes of now) easily meet a 2-hour RPO with no extra scheduling.

others.A: Snapshotting EBS volumes of stateless, constantly scaling instances wastes storage and effort, and manual snapshots every 2 hours are harder to operate.
others.B: EBS snapshot lifecycle policies on stateless instances add cost without value, since nothing unique lives on those volumes.
others.D: Taking EBS snapshots of stateless instances every 2 hours is unnecessary and uses resources poorly.

tip: Stateless tier: back up the AMI, not the volumes.

why: Global customers with dynamic IPs cannot be allowlisted, so the web tier must accept HTTPS (443) from 0.0.0.0/0. The database should accept 3306 only from the web server security group, keeping it unreachable from the internet.

others.B: Customer IP addresses are dynamic and global, so allowlisting them is impossible to maintain.
others.C: Customers should never connect to the database directly, and their dynamic IPs cannot be listed anyway.
others.D: Opening MySQL 3306 to the whole internet is a serious security risk.

why: Amazon Transcribe converts speech to text and has built-in PII redaction for transcripts. Starting a Transcribe job from an S3-triggered Lambda function and writing the redacted output to another bucket is a fully managed, event-driven solution.

others.A: Kinesis Video Streams ingests live video, not stored audio files, and pattern-matching PII yourself in Lambda is fragile.
others.B: Amazon Textract pulls text from documents and images, not audio recordings.
others.D: Amazon Connect is a contact center service; using it to process stored files with custom PII scanning is overly complex.

tip: Speech to text = Transcribe; document OCR = Textract; PII in free text = Comprehend or Transcribe redaction.

why: The workload needs more than 20,000 sustained IOPS with consistent performance. Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) storage is built for I/O-intensive production databases, giving high, predictable IOPS and better durability, so moving the RDS storage to io2 removes the bottleneck.

others.A: Magnetic storage is legacy and much slower, so it would make performance worse.
others.B: On RDS, gp3 volumes of 400 GiB or more can be provisioned well above 20,000 IOPS, so this could work, but the exam expects io2 for sustained high-IOPS production databases.
others.D: RDS manages its own storage layout; you cannot attach two separate gp3 volumes to an RDS instance.

tip: On RDS, gp3 at 400 GiB or more stripes across volumes (baseline 12,000 IOPS, scalable higher); exams still favor io1/io2 for heavy, consistent IOPS.

why: AWS CloudTrail records API calls, including which IAM identity made the call, when, and from where. Looking up AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress and similar events in CloudTrail event history shows who changed the security group rules.

others.A: GuardDuty detects threats from logs; it does not give an audit trail of who made each configuration change.
others.B: Amazon Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities and network exposure, not who made changes.
others.D: AWS Config records how resource configurations change over time, but CloudTrail is the source for which user made the API call.

tip: Who did it = CloudTrail; what changed and is it compliant = Config.

why: AWS Shield Advanced can protect Global Accelerator accelerators directly as protected resources, adding DDoS detection, mitigation and access to the Shield Response Team. Because traffic enters through the accelerator, protecting the accelerator covers the DNS service at its entry point.

others.B: The EC2 instances sit behind the accelerator, so protection belongs on the internet-facing accelerator.
others.C: AWS WAF cannot be associated with Global Accelerator, and WAF handles HTTP layer 7, not DNS/UDP floods.
others.D: WAF cannot be attached directly to EC2 instances, and it does not protect non-HTTP DNS traffic.

tip: Shield Advanced protects CloudFront, Route 53, Global Accelerator, ELB and Elastic IPs; WAF only fronts CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway, AppSync, Cognito and similar HTTP services.

why: The job can run up to an hour and processes objects up to 10 GB, which rules out Lambda's 15-minute limit. An EventBridge scheduled rule that launches an ECS task on AWS Fargate runs the container with known CPU and memory and no servers to manage, minimizing operational effort.

others.A: Lambda functions time out after 15 minutes, so a job of up to an hour cannot run reliably.
others.B: Adding API Gateway does not remove Lambda's 15-minute limit, and API Gateway's integration timeout is also short.
others.D: The EC2 launch type means managing and paying for always-on instances in an Auto Scaling group, which adds overhead.

tip: More than 15 minutes and serverless = Fargate (or AWS Batch on Fargate).

why: At 100 Mbps, 600 TB would take well over a year, so an online transfer cannot finish in 2 weeks. Several Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices (about 80 TB usable each) move the data offline with 256-bit encryption, at a low cost.

others.A: S3 multipart upload over a 100 Mbps link is far too slow for 600 TB in 2 weeks.
others.B: A VPN still runs over the same 100 Mbps internet link, so it is just as slow.
others.D: Direct Connect takes weeks to months to provision, and a 10 Gbps dedicated connection is much more expensive for a one-time move.

tip: Do the math: 100 Mbps moves roughly 1 TB per day.

why: An AWS WAF web ACL with a rate-based rule blocks IP addresses that exceed a set request rate, which directly counters HTTP floods. Regional API Gateway stages can be associated with a regional web ACL natively, so this is a managed solution with the least operational overhead.

others.A: Caching stock prices for 24 hours would serve stale data and does not stop floods of uncacheable or varied requests.
others.C: CloudWatch alarms only alert people and do not block the attack.
others.D: Custom Lambda@Edge rate limiting is complex to build and maintain compared with WAF's built-in rate-based rules.

tip: HTTP flood or too many requests from an IP = WAF rate-based rule.

why: DynamoDB Streams records item changes asynchronously, outside the application's write path, so the current app's performance is unaffected. A Lambda trigger on the stream publishes each new event to one SNS topic, and all four teams subscribe to it, which is the least operational overhead.

others.A: DynamoDB transactions guarantee atomic writes and have no notification feature; they also cost more write capacity.
others.B: Changing the app to publish to four topics adds work to the app's own request path and is more to maintain than one topic.
others.D: Scanning the table every minute uses a lot of read capacity, can slow the app, and means managing a cron job.

tip: React to DynamoDB changes = Streams + Lambda; fan out = one SNS topic with many subscribers.

why: An Auto Scaling group across multiple AZs removes the app tier as a single point of failure and scales with demand. RDS Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby in another AZ with automatic failover, so a crashed database server does not lose committed data.

others.B: A single AZ is a single point of failure, and a database on one EC2 instance can still lose data.
others.C: Read replicas replicate asynchronously and need manual promotion, so data can be lost and failover is not automatic; a single AZ is also a single point of failure.
others.D: EBS Multi-Attach works only within a single AZ and only with io1/io2, so it cannot share storage across AZs; self-managed databases also add overhead.

tip: Survive a DB crash with no data loss = RDS Multi-AZ (synchronous replication).

why: Kinesis Data Streams keeps records for 24 hours by default. Because the consumer only reads every other day, records expire before they are read. Raising the retention period (up to 365 days) keeps the data until the consumer processes it.

others.B: The KPL improves producer throughput and batching, but it does not stop records from expiring before the consumer reads them.
others.C: Adding shards helps throughput problems, but the data loss here comes from the retention window, not throttling.
others.D: S3 Versioning keeps object versions after they arrive; it cannot recover data that never reached S3.

tip: Kinesis Data Streams retention: 24 hours by default, extendable to 7 days, or up to 365 days with long-term retention.

why: Lambda functions should get permissions from an IAM execution role, which supplies temporary credentials that rotate automatically. Attaching a role that grants the needed S3 actions avoids putting long-term IAM user keys in code.

others.A: A Lambda resource-based policy controls who can invoke the function, not what the function can access.
others.B: Putting long-term IAM user credentials in the function to sign requests is insecure and against best practice.
others.C: Making another IAM user and putting its keys in the function has the same problem of hard-coded long-term credentials.

tip: Compute services (EC2, Lambda, ECS) get permissions from roles, never from embedded access keys.

why: A traffic spike can exceed Lambda concurrency limits, and asynchronous S3 invocations that keep failing or are throttled can be dropped. Putting an SQS queue between S3 and Lambda buffers the events durably, so Lambda polls and processes them at a sustainable rate, with retries and an optional dead-letter queue.

others.A: A longer timeout does not fix throttling or dropped events during traffic spikes.
others.B: Replicating the bucket copies objects but adds no reliable processing or retry mechanism.
others.C: Lambda functions cannot be load balanced this way, and a second function draws on the same account concurrency limit.

tip: Bursty event processing = decouple with SQS.

why: Target tracking on average CPU utilization scales the Auto Scaling group out and in automatically as weekday traffic rises and falls. Scheduled actions that set min, max and desired capacity to zero for the weekend and restore them on Monday handle the known downtime pattern.

others.A: ALB capacity scales automatically and cannot be managed with AWS Auto Scaling.
others.B: Internet gateways scale horizontally and are fully managed, so there is nothing to scale.
others.C: Spreading a demo environment across Regions adds complexity and cost and does not deal with daily or weekend patterns.

tip: Predictable time patterns = scheduled scaling; variable load = target tracking.

why: The web servers' security group should allow 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 so internet users can reach them. The DB security group should allow 3306 only from the web servers' security group, which restricts database access to those instances.

others.A: Denying outbound 3306 from the public subnet would block the web servers from reaching the database.
others.B: Allowing the whole public subnet CIDR is broader than allowing only the web server security group.
others.E: Security groups support only allow rules; they cannot contain explicit deny rules.

tip: Security groups: allow only, stateful, can reference other SGs. NACLs: allow and deny, stateless, CIDR-based.

why: Amazon FSx for Lustre is a fully managed, high-performance file system that natively supports the Lustre client. It is the only option that gives Lustre access as a managed service.

others.A: DataSync is a data transfer service and does not provide a mountable file system.
others.B: Storage Gateway file gateways expose NFS or SMB, not Lustre.
others.C: Amazon EFS supports NFS only and cannot be configured to support Lustre.

tip: Lustre/HPC = FSx for Lustre; Windows SMB = FSx for Windows; Linux NFS = EFS.

why: The keyed option's text is cut off. The full intended answer is AWS Global Accelerator with a Network Load Balancer in each Region in front of ECS on Fargate. Global Accelerator sends UDP traffic over the AWS backbone from the nearest edge location to cut latency, and fails over between Regional endpoints in seconds using health checks.

others.A: Route 53 failover depends on DNS TTLs and client caching, so failover is slower, and an NLB cannot invoke Lambda as a target.
others.C: Application Load Balancers support only HTTP and HTTPS, so they cannot accept the devices' UDP traffic.
others.D: ALBs cannot handle UDP, and Route 53 DNS failover is slower than Global Accelerator.

tip: UDP + low global latency + fast Regional failover = Global Accelerator + NLB.
flag: Option B's text is truncated in the source data; the intended correct option is Global Accelerator with NLB endpoints in two Regions targeting ECS Fargate.

why: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server is a managed, native SMB file system that IIS on Windows can use directly. A Multi-AZ deployment replicates data across AZs with automatic failover, making it the most resilient and durable replacement for the NAS file share.

others.A: Amazon RDS is a relational database, not a file share.
others.B: Storage Gateway is for hybrid access from on premises and adds a gateway appliance that can become a point of failure for EC2 workloads in AWS.
others.D: Amazon EFS uses NFS and is not supported on Windows instances.

tip: Windows file share in AWS = FSx for Windows File Server (pick Multi-AZ for resilience).

why: Creating the EBS volumes as encrypted (with KMS) encrypts data at rest, plus snapshots and data moving between the instance and the volume. Turning on EBS encryption by default for the account and Region also enforces this for new volumes.

others.A: IAM roles grant permissions; they cannot make volumes encrypted.
others.C: Tags are just metadata and do not cause any encryption.
others.D: KMS key policies control who can use a key; they cannot force EBS volumes to be encrypted.

tip: An unencrypted volume cannot be encrypted in place: snapshot it, copy the snapshot with encryption, then create a new volume.

why: Aurora Serverless is MySQL-compatible, so no database changes are needed. It scales capacity up and down automatically for spiky, unpredictable usage, and you pay only for the capacity you use, which is cost-effective for this pattern.

others.A: DynamoDB is a NoSQL database and would require rewriting the application's data layer.
others.B: A provisioned RDS for MySQL instance must be sized for peak load, so it wastes money during quiet periods.
others.D: MySQL on EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group cannot simply scale out a relational database and means heavy self-management.

tip: Unpredictable or intermittent relational load = Aurora Serverless v2.

why: Account-level S3 Block Public Access overrides any bucket policy or ACL that would make objects public, across every bucket in the account. An SCP that denies s3:PutAccountPublicAccessBlock stops anyone from turning the setting off, which prevents accidental exposure instead of fixing it afterward.

others.A: GuardDuty detects threats and does not monitor or remediate bucket policies the way described, and remediation after the fact still allows exposure.
others.B: Trusted Advisor checks and manual fixes are reactive and leave a window of exposure.
others.C: AWS Resource Access Manager shares resources across accounts and does not detect public S3 buckets.

tip: Prevent public S3 = Block Public Access (account level) + SCP to lock it.

why: Amazon SES is a managed email-sending service that handles deliverability, bounces, complaints, reputation and scaling. Sending through SES via its API or SMTP removes the effort of running email infrastructure and fixing delivery problems.

others.A: A dedicated email tier on EC2 still leaves the team running mail servers and debugging delivery issues.
others.C: SNS email notifications are for simple topic alerts to subscribers and do not support custom transactional or marketing email.
others.D: Adding Auto Scaling to self-managed email servers still keeps all the operational burden.

tip: Transactional or marketing email = SES.

why: An Amazon S3 File Gateway presents an SMB or NFS share on premises and uploads each file it writes to S3 as an object, in near-real time. Pointing the business system at the new share needs no scheduling or custom code.

others.A: A daily DataSync task is batch, not near-real time.
others.C: Writing an application around the DataSync API adds development and maintenance effort.
others.D: A custom script that watches the share and uploads over SFTP is extra code to build and maintain.

tip: On-prem app writes to a file share, data should land in S3 = S3 File Gateway.

why: S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves each object between frequent, infrequent and archive instant access tiers based on its actual access, with no retrieval fees. A lifecycle rule that sends objects to Intelligent-Tiering is a hands-off way to optimize cost when access patterns are unknown.

others.B: Running storage class analysis and moving each object by hand across petabytes takes a lot of ongoing effort.
others.C: Glacier Instant Retrieval has higher retrieval costs, so frequently accessed objects would cost more.
others.D: One Zone-IA lowers durability across AZs and charges retrieval fees, which is bad for frequently accessed data.

tip: Unknown or changing access patterns = S3 Intelligent-Tiering.

why: CloudFront caches static and dynamic content at edge locations close to global users, which cuts page load times. An RDS read replica takes read queries off the primary database, easing database contention behind slow dynamic pages.

others.A: Redshift is a data warehouse for analytics and does not speed up OLTP page loads.
others.C: S3 can host only static content; it cannot run dynamic web content.
others.E: Multi-AZ improves availability and does not serve reads or improve performance.

why: The keyed option's text is garbled. The intended answer is a Compute Savings Plan, optimizing Lambda duration, memory and invocations, and connecting the Lambda functions to the private subnet that holds the EC2 instances. Compute Savings Plans cover both EC2 and Lambda for up to 66 percent savings, and VPC-attached functions reach the instances privately with low latency.

others.A: EC2 Instance Savings Plans cover only EC2 in one instance family and Region, so they do not save anything on the growing Lambda usage.
others.B: EC2 Instance Savings Plans do not cover Lambda, and putting Lambda in a public subnet gives it no internet access or benefit.
others.D: Lambda functions left in the Lambda service VPC cannot reach EC2 instances in the company's private subnet directly.

tip: Savings across EC2, Fargate and Lambda = Compute Savings Plan.
flag: Option C's text is missing in the source data; the intended correct option is Compute Savings Plan + optimize Lambda + connect Lambda to the private subnet with the EC2 instances.

why: Cross-account access should use role assumption. Adding the development account as a trusted principal in the production role's trust policy lets the existing development users (with sts:AssumeRole permission) assume the role and get only its S3 permissions.

others.A: AdministratorAccess grants far more than S3 access and still does not give access to the production account.
others.C: Turning off Block Public Access would expose the bucket publicly, which is insecure and unnecessary.
others.D: Duplicate users in production mean more credentials to manage instead of reusing roles.

tip: Cross-account access = IAM role with a trust policy + sts:AssumeRole.

why: An SCP on the root OU that denies ec2:CreateVolume when ec2:Encrypted is false blocks unencrypted volumes in member accounts, including for their root users. Pairing it with default EBS encryption means volumes are encrypted automatically, so employees are not disrupted.

others.A: The EBS encryption-by-default account attribute works, but it must be set in each account and Region; the key prefers the organization-wide pairing.
others.B: Permission boundaries attach to IAM users and roles, not to OUs, and they do not affect the root user.
others.D: Editing IAM policies in every account is error-prone and does not restrict the root user.

tip: SCPs restrict even the root user of member accounts, but never the management account.
flag: EBS encryption by default is a per-account, per-Region EC2 setting; there is no Organizations-wide default EBS encryption setting, so A + C is more accurate than C + E.

why: An RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment has a writer and two readable standby instances in different AZs, with automatic failover typically under 35 seconds. The reader endpoint spreads read traffic across the standbys, offloading the primary without paying for extra read replicas.

others.A: Multi-AZ DB instance failover usually takes 60 to 120 seconds, and the extra read replica adds cost.
others.B: Multi-AZ DB clusters already have readable standbys, so two more read replicas add unnecessary cost.
others.C: In a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment the standby cannot serve read traffic.

tip: Multi-AZ DB instance: 1 standby that cannot serve reads. Multi-AZ DB cluster: 2 readable standbys, faster failover.

why: AWS Transfer Family is a serverless SFTP service. Backing it with Amazon EFS gives shared POSIX storage with high IOPS and keeps control of user permissions through POSIX UID/GID. A VPC-hosted, internet-facing endpoint with Elastic IPs lets you attach a security group that allows only trusted source IPs, which gives highly configurable security.

others.A: Transfer Family supports only S3 or EFS as storage; you cannot attach an EBS volume, and public endpoints cannot use security groups.
others.C: A public Transfer Family endpoint cannot restrict source IPs with security groups, and S3 does not offer the file-level POSIX permissions and IOPS profile the question asks for.
others.D: An internal-only VPC endpoint in a private subnet cannot be reached by trusted clients on the internet.

tip: Transfer Family source-IP filtering = VPC endpoint (internet-facing with EIPs) + security group.

why: An SQS queue absorbs irregular, bursty asynchronous requests. ECS services that poll the queue can load the 1 GB of model data into memory once per task, and ECS service auto scaling plus cluster capacity scaling, based on queue depth, scale out for big batches and in when idle.

others.A: An NLB cannot invoke Lambda functions (only an ALB can), and the API is asynchronous, so a load balancer is the wrong front end.
others.B: AWS App Mesh is a service mesh for traffic routing; it does not scale ECS based on queue size, and an ALB does not fit an asynchronous queue-based API.
others.C: You cannot scale Lambda vCPUs with Auto Scaling; vCPU follows the memory setting, and reloading 1 GB of model data on cold starts is inefficient.

tip: Queue-depth scaling of workers = SQS + ECS service auto scaling (backlog per task).

why: Identity-based policies attach to IAM identities: users, groups and roles. Of the options, only Role and Group are IAM identities that can hold an identity-based policy.

others.C: An organization is governed by SCPs, not identity-based IAM policies.
others.D: An ECS resource is not an IAM principal; ECS tasks get permissions through an IAM task role.
others.E: An EC2 instance gets permissions through an instance profile containing a role; the policy attaches to the role, not to the instance.

tip: Identity-based policies attach to users, groups and roles; resource-based policies attach to resources like S3 buckets.

why: Frontend nodes run 24/7, so Reserved Instances (or Savings Plans) give the biggest discount for steady usage. Backend nodes run briefly and vary with workload, which fits Spot Instances at up to 90 percent off, assuming the work can tolerate interruption.

others.A: Fargate would mean containerizing the backend, and it usually costs more per compute unit than Spot EC2 for the same work.
others.C: Spot Instances can be interrupted, which is unsuitable for always-on frontend nodes, and RIs waste money on part-time backend nodes.
others.D: Spot is unsuitable for the always-on frontend, and Fargate is not the cheapest option for the backend.

tip: Steady 24/7 = RI or Savings Plan; short and flexible = Spot.

why: gp3 volumes let you provision IOPS (up to 16,000) and throughput separately from capacity, with a 3,000 IOPS baseline at any size. They cost about 20 percent less per GB than gp2, so they are the most cost-effective choice for a 15,000 IOPS peak.

others.A: gp2 IOPS are tied to volume size (3 IOPS per GB), so performance cannot be provisioned independently of capacity.
others.B: io2 meets the need but costs much more than gp3 for only 15,000 IOPS.
others.D: io1 is also more expensive than gp3 and offers no benefit at this IOPS level.

tip: 16,000 IOPS or less and independent of size = gp3; above that or sub-millisecond critical = io2 Block Express.

why: AWS DataSync transfers the existing data to S3 online, securely (TLS) and quickly, with integrity checks. It can also handle the changing data with incremental syncs. CloudTrail data events record object-level S3 API activity (GetObject, PutObject), which gives the audit access at all levels that the regulation requires.

others.B: Snowcone holds only 8 to 14 TB and is offline, and CloudTrail management events do not capture object-level access.
others.C: S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads but is not a migration tool with scheduling and verification for a large dataset.
others.D: CloudTrail management events do not log object-level reads and writes, so they fail the audit requirement.

tip: Object-level S3 auditing = CloudTrail data events (management events cover control-plane calls only).

why: Elastic Beanstalk has a managed Tomcat platform for Java apps. A load-balanced environment runs instances behind an ELB in an Auto Scaling group across multiple AZs for high availability, and rolling deployments update without full downtime.

others.A: Lambda cannot host a complex Tomcat-based application without major refactoring.
others.C: ElastiCache is an in-memory cache, not a replacement for a MySQL relational database.
others.D: Putting MySQL on the same instance as the app means each scaled copy has its own separate database, which breaks data consistency and leaves no HA database.

tip: Deploy a web app on a familiar stack (Tomcat, .NET, Node) with little ops work = Elastic Beanstalk.

why: The secure pattern is an IAM role that trusts the Lambda service (lambda.amazonaws.com), carries a least-privilege DynamoDB policy, and is set as the function's execution role. Lambda then gets temporary credentials that rotate automatically, with no stored keys.

others.A: Long-term access keys in environment variables can leak and must be rotated by hand.
others.C: Parameter Store protects the keys better, but this still relies on long-term IAM user credentials instead of a role.
others.D: The trust policy must trust the Lambda service, not DynamoDB, and roles are set in the function configuration, not attached from code.

why: The policy image is not shown, but it allows all EC2 actions in us-east-1 and allows (or conditions) StopInstances and TerminateInstances on MFA being present. IAM evaluates all statements together. The effect is that members can do any EC2 action in us-east-1, and stop or terminate instances there only when they signed in with MFA.

others.A: IAM does not stop at the first matching statement; all statements are evaluated, and an explicit deny or condition still applies.
others.B: The MFA condition applies only to stop and terminate, not to every EC2 action.
others.C: The Region condition limits permissions to us-east-1, so they do not apply in all Regions.

tip: IAM evaluation: explicit deny beats allow, allow beats the implicit deny, and statement order does not matter.

why: An S3 event-triggered Lambda function converts each .csv to an image as soon as it arrives, with no idle compute. Lifecycle rules move the .csv files to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 1 day, which is cheap and acceptable because trainings are planned weeks ahead, and expire images after 30 days.

others.A: An hourly Spot Instance batch adds delay instead of making images available as soon as possible, and Spot can be interrupted.
others.D: One Zone-IA costs more than Glacier for data read only twice a year and has lower resilience.
others.E: Standard-IA costs more than Glacier for rarely read data, and Reduced Redundancy Storage is deprecated and does not expire images.

tip: Retrieval planned weeks ahead = Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive.

why: ElastiCache for Redis sorted sets (ZADD, ZREVRANGE) compute a live top-10 leaderboard in memory with very low latency. Redis also supports persistence (snapshots/AOF) and backup and restore, so scores survive stopping and restoring the game.

others.A: Memcached has no sorted sets, persistence or backup and restore, so it cannot reliably keep scores.
others.C: CloudFront caching would serve stale scoreboards and does not compute rankings.
others.D: Running ranking queries over and over on a MySQL read replica is slower and adds replication lag compared with an in-memory sorted set.

why: Amazon SageMaker is the managed service for building, training and deploying ML models. Amazon QuickSight is the managed BI service that can visualize the augmented data, and it integrates with SageMaker models for ML-powered insights, with the least operational overhead.

others.A: AWS Glue ML transforms only find matching or duplicate records, and OpenSearch dashboards are not a BI reporting platform.
others.C: Running your own ML AMIs on EC2 means managing infrastructure, which adds overhead.
others.D: QuickSight calculated fields cannot build and train custom ML models.

why: Service control policies set preventive guardrails across accounts in AWS Organizations. An SCP that denies tag-changing actions for the cost allocation tag keys, with a condition exempting authorized principals, stops changes before they happen in every member account.

others.A: AWS Config rules detect and report noncompliance after the fact; they do not prevent changes.
others.B: CloudTrail only logs API activity; it cannot block changes.
others.D: CloudWatch Logs stores logs and cannot prevent tag changes.

tip: Prevent across accounts = SCP (or tag policies for enforcing tag values); detect = Config.

why: A warm standby, with an Auto Scaling group and load balancer already running in the DR Region, plus a DynamoDB global table that is already replicating data, keeps both tiers ready. Route 53 DNS failover health checks switch traffic automatically, giving the least downtime.

others.B: Building EC2, load balancers and an empty DynamoDB table from CloudFormation at failover time takes time and has no replicated data.
others.C: Launching compute from a template during an outage still adds provisioning time compared with infrastructure that is already running.
others.D: A custom CloudWatch alarm plus Lambda to update Route 53 reinvents built-in Route 53 failover routing and adds delay and moving parts.

tip: Least downtime across Regions = pre-provisioned resources + global tables + Route 53 failover.

why: A Snowball Edge Storage Optimized device (about 80 TB) moves the 20 TB full load offline cheaply within 2 weeks, using DMS with the device as the target. DMS change data capture then replicates ongoing changes after the data is loaded into AWS, keeping downtime minimal.

others.B: Snowmobile was for exabyte-scale transfers (and is retired), which is far too much for 20 TB.
others.C: Compute Optimized with GPU devices cost more and target edge computing, not bulk storage transfer.
others.D: Direct Connect usually takes longer than 2 weeks to provision and costs more for a one-time migration.

tip: Large DB migration with little downtime and limited bandwidth = Snowball Edge + DMS with CDC.

why: Scaling the existing RDS instance up to a larger class handles more load without adding infrastructure. Buying Reserved DB instances for the steady load gives up to about 69 percent savings over On-Demand, which makes it the most cost-effective option.

others.B: Multi-AZ adds a standby for availability that cannot serve traffic, so it adds cost without adding capacity.
others.C: Adding another DB instance means adding infrastructure, which the company wants to avoid.
others.D: On-Demand pricing is the most expensive option for a steady, ongoing workload and adds no capacity.

why: AWS WAF attached to the ALB with a rate-based rule blocks clients that exceed a request threshold, whatever their changing IP addresses, while normal-rate legitimate users pass through. Managed rule groups such as IP reputation lists can block known bad sources too.

others.A: Amazon Inspector scans for vulnerabilities and cannot block incoming requests.
others.C: Network ACLs apply to subnets, need static CIDR entries and have rule limits, so they cannot keep up with changing IPs.
others.D: GuardDuty detects threats but has no rate-limiting or blocking feature.

why: Sharing an encrypted RDS snapshot with the auditor's AWS account, and granting that account access to the customer managed KMS key, lets the auditor restore its own copy. Data stays encrypted, no credentials are shared, and the database is never exposed.

others.A: A read replica stays in the company's account and network, and the auditor needs its own copy, not access to company infrastructure.
others.B: Exporting to text files and creating IAM users loses the database format and adds credential management.
others.C: RDS snapshots cannot simply be copied as files to S3 this way, and sharing IAM user keys is insecure.

tip: Encrypted snapshots can be shared only when encrypted with a customer managed KMS key whose policy grants the other account access.

why: A VPC can have secondary IPv4 CIDR blocks added (up to 5 by default) without disrupting existing resources. Creating new subnets from the added range gives more IP addresses with the least operational overhead.

others.B: A second VPC with peering means more routing, security group and network management.
others.C: This entry is a data artifact rather than a real answer choice.
others.D: Creating a second VPC (the text is cut off) adds more networking overhead than extending the current VPC.

tip: Out of IPs = add a secondary CIDR to the VPC.

why: An RDS for MySQL snapshot can be restored or migrated directly to an Aurora MySQL DB cluster from the console or CLI. A logical dump can also be loaded into Aurora MySQL; Aurora's native S3 import expects Percona XtraBackup files, but the exam treats staging the dump in S3 and importing it as valid.

others.B: RDS snapshots are managed by AWS and cannot be uploaded or exported to S3 as an importable file for Aurora.
others.D: DMS migrates from live source databases or supported files, not from RDS snapshots.
others.E: DMS cannot use a mysqldump file in S3 as a source.

tip: RDS MySQL to Aurora MySQL: restore the snapshot as Aurora, or create an Aurora read replica and promote it.

why: Static content is what drives the unnecessary scale-out. Serving it from S3 through CloudFront moves that load off the EC2 fleet and caches it at edge locations, so fewer instances are needed and users get lower latency. That is the most cost-effective redesign.

others.A: Reserved Instances only discount instances; they do not stop the fleet from scaling to serve static files, and RIs suit steady usage rather than bursts.
others.B: Spot Instances make each instance cheaper, but the architecture still wastes compute on static files and risks interruptions.
others.D: Lambda with API Gateway is a poor and costly way to serve static files compared with S3 and CloudFront.

tip: Static content = S3 + CloudFront; keep the compute for dynamic requests.

why: Lake Formation tag-based access control (LF-TBAC) assigns LF-Tags to databases, tables and columns, then grants permissions on tag expressions, including to other accounts. This shares selected data across accounts at scale without copying data or managing grants on each resource.

others.A: Copying petabytes into a common account is expensive and duplicates data that must then be kept in sync.
others.B: Named-resource grants in every account must be maintained one by one and do not scale well.
others.C: AWS Data Exchange is meant for publishing data products to subscribers, which is overkill for internal sharing within a Lake Formation data lake.

tip: Lake Formation sharing at scale = LF-Tags (TBAC).

why: S3 Transfer Acceleration sends uploads and downloads through CloudFront edge locations and over the AWS backbone, which speeds up long-distance transfers of large, unique objects. Users pay the extra per-GB fee only when acceleration actually helps, which keeps it cost-effective.

others.B: CacheControl headers only affect caching; they do nothing for unique uploads or long-distance transfer speed.
others.C: CloudFront helps cacheable downloads, but unique GB-sized objects get little benefit, and running EC2 plus Auto Scaling costs more.
others.D: ElastiCache is an in-memory cache inside the Region and does not reduce global network latency for large file transfers.

tip: Fast global uploads to S3 = Transfer Acceleration; for very large files add multipart upload.

why: RDS deletion protection prevents accidental deletion, and Multi-AZ adds a synchronous standby with automatic failover. Putting the web servers in an Auto Scaling group across multiple AZs behind an ALB removes the single-AZ and manual-instance weak points, which maximizes reliability.

others.A: Cutting down to one EC2 instance in one AZ makes reliability worse.
others.C: Writing to two DB instances through API Gateway and Lambda is a fragile, custom replication scheme that does not prevent deletion.
others.D: Spot Instances can be interrupted, which hurts reliability, and there is no load balancer to spread traffic across AZs.

why: AWS DataSync runs online transfers over the existing 10 Gbps Direct Connect, and can move 700 TB well within 90 days. It does incremental syncs, so the NAS stays available and editable during the transfer and changes are copied in later passes, with encryption and integrity checks.

others.B: Snowball is offline, so changes made after copying would be missed, and you cannot mount an S3 bucket on the on-prem file system this way.
others.C: rsync cannot write to S3 directly and lacks DataSync's parallel transfers, checks and management.
others.D: Tapes are slow, offline and cannot capture ongoing updates.

tip: Good bandwidth + data changing during the move = DataSync.

why: S3 Object Lock in compliance mode means no user, including root, can delete or overwrite object versions during the 7-year retention period, which meets the legal requirement. S3 Batch Operations can apply Object Lock retention to existing objects in bulk, without recopying them, for the least operational overhead.

others.A: Versioning with MFA delete and lifecycle rules does not legally lock data, and privileged users can still delete it.
others.B: Governance mode can be bypassed by users with special permissions, and recopying every object is high effort.
others.C: Compliance mode is right, but recopying all existing objects takes more effort than Batch Operations.

tip: Legal or regulatory WORM = Object Lock compliance mode; existing objects = S3 Batch Operations.

why: Deploying the API Gateway and Lambda stack in several Regions, then using Route 53 records (latency or weighted) with health checks, routes users to healthy Regions and stops sending traffic to an unhealthy one. This active-active setup gives Regional failover for a stateless app.

others.B: CloudFront origin failover is based on error responses rather than health checks, and it works only as primary/secondary origin groups, not multi-Region active routing.
others.C: Transit Gateway connects VPCs and on-prem networks; it cannot attach to or route requests to API Gateway endpoints.
others.D: An ALB in one Region is a single Regional point of failure and cannot target API Gateway hostnames.

why: The keyed option's text is missing. The intended answer is to add a second set of VPNs to the Management VPC from a second customer gateway device. The Management VPC's VPN ends on a single on-prem device, which is its single point of failure, and a second customer gateway removes it.

others.A: VPNs between two VPCs are not needed; the peering connection is a redundant managed service, not a single point of failure.
others.B: Only one virtual private gateway can be attached to a VPC, and the weak point is the single customer device anyway.
others.D: VPC peering is not a single point of failure, and you cannot create a second active peering connection between the same two VPCs.

tip: VPN redundancy = two customer gateway devices; each AWS VPN connection already has two tunnels.
flag: Option C's text is missing in the source data; the intended correct option is adding a second set of VPNs from a second customer gateway device to the Management VPC.

why: Amazon RDS Custom for Oracle gives privileged (OS and SYSDBA) access so third-party features can be installed and configured, while AWS still automates backups and much of the administration. That meets the need for privileged access with less effort and cost than running Oracle on EC2.

others.A: Standard RDS for Oracle gives no privileged access, and replacing the third-party features would slow the migration.
others.C: Oracle on EC2 means the company handles all backups, patching and HA, which it lacks resources for.
others.D: Rewriting for PostgreSQL is slow and costly and does not suit a quick migration.

tip: Managed database but needs OS or privileged access = RDS Custom (Oracle or SQL Server).

why: Refactoring into separate web, app and database tiers in private subnets across two AZs, with Auto Scaling, gives scalability and resilience. ELBs in front of the web tier, with security groups that reference each tier's security group, enforce least-privilege access. An RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster in private subnets that accepts connections only from the app tier makes the data layer highly available and secure.

others.A: Lifting the monolith onto EC2 unchanged does not separate tiers and does not follow best practices.
others.B: A single RDS database is a single point of failure, which goes against resiliency guidance.
others.D: A single RDS database has no high availability.

why: Under the shared responsibility model, customers create RDS instances and choose maintenance windows. Customers configure software on ECS container instances (EC2 launch type), such as monitoring, patching, logging and host intrusion detection. Customers also encrypt data in transit over Direct Connect, which is not encrypted by default, for example by using MACsec or a VPN.

others.A: AWS manages the RDS infrastructure, operating system and database platform.
others.D: AWS applies RDS database engine patches (customers only choose the timing or opt in to version upgrades).
others.E: AWS is responsible for physical security of its data centers.

tip: Direct Connect is private but not encrypted; use MACsec or a Site-to-Site VPN over it.

why: A 10-second hourly job with 1 GB of memory is ideal for Lambda: an EventBridge schedule invokes it, and you pay only for about 10 seconds of compute per hour instead of an idle instance. Lambda assigns CPU in proportion to memory, which is enough for the short CPU bursts.

others.A: Fargate works but has per-task startup overhead and a 1-minute billing minimum, and containerizing adds effort compared with Lambda.
others.C: Running the container on the existing EC2 AMI still keeps an instance running and paid for.
others.D: Stopping and starting EC2 every hour adds boot time and complexity, and per-second billing with a 1-minute minimum still costs more than Lambda.

tip: Short, scheduled, under 15 minutes = Lambda + EventBridge Scheduler.

why: AWS Backup centrally backs up EC2 and S3. Vault Lock in compliance mode makes recovery points immutable: once the grace period ends, no one, including root, can delete them or shorten retention, which meets the requirement that files cannot be altered during the retention period.

others.A: Governance mode can be bypassed or removed by users with sufficient IAM permissions, so it does not guarantee immutability.
others.B: Data Lifecycle Manager handles only EBS snapshots and AMIs, not S3, and does not lock them.
others.C: S3 File Gateway is for hybrid file access, not a backup solution with immutable retention.

tip: Immutable backups for regulators = AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode.

why: Workload Discovery on AWS is an AWS Solution that crawls resources across accounts and Regions using AWS Config and builds architecture diagrams showing resource relationships automatically. It is the most operationally efficient way to inventory and map undocumented workloads.

others.A: Systems Manager Inventory collects software and configuration data from managed instances and does not map relationships between workloads.
others.B: Collecting data with Step Functions and drawing diagrams by hand is slow and error-prone.
others.D: X-Ray traces requests through instrumented applications, not resources across all accounts.

why: Create budgets with AWS Budgets in the Billing console. Budget actions need an IAM role that AWS Budgets can assume to run them. Configure an alert and a budget action that applies an SCP to the target accounts when the threshold is reached, which stops new resources from being provisioned.

others.A: Budgets are not set inside Cost and Usage Reports, which are detailed billing exports.
others.C: AWS Budgets uses an IAM role it assumes, not an IAM user.
others.E: AWS Config rules detect noncompliance; they are not a budget action type and cannot block provisioning.

tip: Budget actions can apply an IAM policy, apply an SCP, or stop EC2/RDS instances.

why: AWS Backup centrally manages EC2 backups from one account and can copy recovery points to a second Region automatically with cross-Region copy rules. You can then restore instances there when needed, without paying for standby compute, which makes it the most cost-effective option.

others.A: Running a similar fleet in the second Region costs a lot for a backup requirement.
others.B: Copying snapshots periodically by hand takes manual effort, does not give central backup management, and EBS snapshots alone do not capture full instance AMIs.
others.D: Running duplicate instances plus DataSync is costly, and DataSync is not an EC2 backup tool.

why: AWS Transfer Family supports the AS2 protocol for business-to-business data exchange. It can use a custom identity provider through a Lambda function (or API Gateway) so the company's own IdP authenticates users.

others.A: DataSync moves data between storage systems and does not support AS2.
others.B: Amazon AppFlow moves data between SaaS apps and AWS services and does not support AS2.
others.D: Storage Gateway offers file, volume and tape interfaces, not AS2.

tip: SFTP, FTPS, FTP or AS2 = AWS Transfer Family.

why: Lambda supports up to 10 GB of memory and up to 10 GB of ephemeral /tmp storage, so 1 GB of memory and 2 GB of storage fit serverless compute behind API Gateway. Amazon RDS gives managed relational storage, which together requires the least administrative effort.

others.A: EC2 means managing servers, patching and scaling.
others.D: DynamoDB is a NoSQL key-value store, not relational.
others.E: EKS means running and operating Kubernetes, which takes much more admin effort.

why: Cost allocation tags are activated from the management (payer) account of the organization. Since department is a tag the company created, it is a user-defined tag. After activating it, one Cost Explorer report grouped by the department tag and filtered to EC2 shows spending across all accounts.

others.B: AWS-generated tags use the aws: prefix (like aws:createdBy); department is user-defined.
others.C: In an organization, only the management account can activate cost allocation tags.
others.D: It is both the wrong account and the wrong tag type.

tip: Cost allocation tags: activate in the management account; user-defined vs AWS-generated (aws: prefix).

why: Amazon AppFlow is a fully managed integration service with a native Salesforce connector. It transfers data to S3 over TLS (encrypted in transit) and encrypts data at rest with KMS customer managed keys, and it can use AWS PrivateLink.

others.A: Custom Lambda code to call Salesforce APIs must be built and maintained, including handling authentication and pagination.
others.B: Step Functions orchestrates tasks but still needs custom code to do the Salesforce transfer.
others.D: A custom connector is unnecessary because AppFlow already includes a managed Salesforce connector.

tip: SaaS (Salesforce, SAP, Slack, Zendesk) to S3 or Redshift = Amazon AppFlow.

why: The keyed option's text is a leftover fragment. The intended answer is AWS Global Accelerator in front of a Network Load Balancer that listens on the TCP and UDP ports, with the Auto Scaling group registering instances on the NLB. Global Accelerator carries both TCP and UDP from the nearest edge location over the AWS backbone, giving the lowest global latency, and only an NLB supports UDP.

others.A: Application Load Balancers support only HTTP and HTTPS, so they cannot listen on UDP ports.
others.C: CloudFront supports only HTTP and HTTPS (plus WebSocket), not arbitrary TCP or UDP game traffic.
others.D: CloudFront cannot carry UDP, and ALBs cannot listen on UDP.

tip: Non-HTTP TCP/UDP with global low latency = Global Accelerator + NLB.
flag: Option B's text is a garbled fragment in the source data; the intended correct option is Global Accelerator with an NLB listening on TCP and UDP.

why: Writing orders to an SQS queue stores each order durably right away, even during spikes. A fleet of EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group pulls from the queue and writes to Aurora, scaling with load so orders are processed reliably and as quickly as capacity allows.

others.A: SNS cannot deliver messages to a database endpoint, and a bigger instance does not decouple or buffer load.
others.C: SNS is push-based and does not keep messages for workers to poll, and a database cannot subscribe to a topic.
others.D: Queueing only after hitting a CPU threshold adds complexity, and scheduled scaling does not react to unpredictable spikes.

tip: Reliable buffering of bursty writes = SQS + Auto Scaling consumers (scale on queue depth).

why: Each job uses 1 GB of memory and finishes in 30 seconds, well within Lambda's 10 GB and 15-minute limits. An S3 event can invoke a Python Lambda function as soon as data arrives, and you pay only per millisecond of execution, which makes it the most cost-effective choice.

others.A: Glue Spark jobs have startup latency and DPU-based minimum billing, which is overkill for 2 MB files.
others.B: EMR clusters cost far more and take much more effort to run for tiny, short jobs.
others.D: PySpark on Glue has the same startup and minimum-cost drawbacks as other Glue Spark jobs.

tip: Small, short, event-driven processing = Lambda.

why: Modifying the existing RDS instance to Multi-AZ creates a synchronous standby in another AZ with automatic failover. The DB endpoint DNS name does not change, so no application code changes are needed, and the conversion happens online with minimal impact.

others.B: Restoring from a snapshot creates a new endpoint, so the app config must change, and writes made after the snapshot are lost or need a cutover.
others.C: Read replicas are read-only and replicate asynchronously, so weighted routing would send writes to a replica that cannot accept them.
others.D: RDS instances cannot be put in EC2 Auto Scaling groups.

tip: Single-AZ to Multi-AZ is a simple modify operation with the same endpoint.

why: EBS Multi-Attach lets one volume attach to up to 16 Nitro-based instances in the same AZ, with simultaneous read and write access. It is supported only on Provisioned IOPS SSD volumes (io1 and io2), so io2 is the right choice.

others.A: gp3 volumes do not support Multi-Attach.
others.B: st1 HDD volumes do not support Multi-Attach.
others.D: gp2 volumes do not support Multi-Attach.

tip: Multi-Attach = io1/io2 only, same AZ only, needs a cluster-aware file system.

why: The database is already Multi-AZ, so the remaining single point of failure is the EC2 tier in one AZ. A Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer spreads the stateless instances across AZs and replaces unhealthy ones, which makes the application highly available.

others.B: Cross-Region snapshots are a backup or DR measure; they do not keep the application available in real time.
others.C: Latency-based routing does not help when every instance is in one AZ.
others.D: A Multi-AZ ALB alone does not help if all EC2 instances are still in one AZ, and Route 53 rules add nothing here.

why: In AWS Organizations, Savings Plans and Reserved Instance discount sharing is controlled from the management account's billing preferences. Turning sharing on there lets unused Compute Savings Plan commitment apply to eligible usage in other accounts in the organization.

others.A: Member accounts cannot turn on organization-wide discount sharing; the setting lives in the management account.
others.C: Migrating workloads between accounts is disruptive, high-effort work just to use a discount that sharing handles automatically.
others.D: Savings Plans cannot be sold; only certain Standard Reserved Instances can be sold on the Reserved Instance Marketplace.

why: Amazon API Gateway REST APIs meet the REST requirement. A private VPC link (through an NLB, or for HTTP APIs an ALB or Cloud Map) lets API Gateway reach ECS services in private subnets without exposing them to the internet.

others.A: WebSocket APIs are for two-way persistent connections, not the REST interface that is required.
others.C: WebSocket is the wrong API type, and API Gateway does not sit in your VPC with a security group.
others.D: API Gateway is a managed service outside your VPC, so a security group alone cannot give it access to private subnets.

tip: API Gateway to private VPC resources = VPC link.

why: When access patterns cannot be predicted or controlled, S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between access tiers based on their actual use, with no retrieval fees. A lifecycle rule to transition objects into Intelligent-Tiering cuts cost without guessing.

others.A: S3 Replication copies objects to other buckets; it is not a tiering mechanism.
others.B: Moving objects to Standard-IA on a fixed schedule can lead to retrieval fees and minimum storage charges when objects are accessed often after all.
others.D: S3 Inventory lists objects but does not show access and does not transition anything, so it needs manual work.

why: An egress-only internet gateway is the IPv6 equivalent of a NAT gateway. It allows outbound IPv6 connections to the internet and blocks inbound connections started from outside, which matches the security policy.

others.A: NAT gateways do NAT for IPv4 (plus NAT64), not native IPv6 egress.
others.B: An internet gateway allows two-way IPv6 traffic, so external hosts could start connections.
others.C: A virtual private gateway connects to on-premises networks over VPN, not to the internet.

tip: IPv4 outbound only = NAT gateway; IPv6 outbound only = egress-only IGW.

why: The keyed option's text is cut off; the intended answer is to create a gateway VPC endpoint for S3 and associate it with all route tables in the VPC. Gateway endpoints for S3 cost nothing and keep traffic on the AWS network, which avoids NAT gateway data processing charges on 1 TB a day.

others.A: Intelligent-Tiering changes storage costs but does not keep traffic off the internet.
others.B: Transfer Acceleration adds cost and still uses public endpoints over the internet edge.
others.D: Interface endpoints for S3 charge hourly and per-GB fees, so they cost more than a free gateway endpoint for traffic from within the VPC.

tip: S3 or DynamoDB from inside a VPC = gateway endpoint (free); from on prem = interface endpoint.
flag: Option C's text is truncated in the source data; the intended correct option is creating an S3 gateway VPC endpoint associated with all route tables.

why: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is an in-memory cache built for DynamoDB that brings reads from milliseconds to microseconds. It is API-compatible with DynamoDB, so the app only needs to point the DynamoDB client at the DAX endpoint, which means minimal code changes.

others.B: This entry is a data artifact rather than a real answer choice.
others.C: More read capacity reduces throttling but does not lower per-request read latency below DynamoDB's single-digit milliseconds.
others.D: ElastiCache for Redis needs cache-aside logic and significant code changes compared with DAX.

tip: Microsecond DynamoDB reads with few code changes = DAX.

why: A CloudFront distribution caches static files at edge locations, so most requests never reach the ALB and EC2 instances. CloudFront data transfer out is also usually cheaper than from EC2 or ALB, so cost stays down as traffic grows.

others.B: WAF web ACLs filter requests; they cannot cache content.
others.C: Attaching a WAF web ACL to the ALB adds cost and does nothing for caching or load.
others.D: A second ALB and fleet in another Region roughly doubles infrastructure cost.

why: AWS Transit Gateway acts as a Regional hub that connects many VPCs without a full mesh of peering connections. Inter-Region Transit Gateway peering links the hubs, giving any-to-any connectivity across Regions with the least administrative effort.

others.A: Full-mesh VPC peering needs n(n-1)/2 connections and route updates because peering is not transitive, which is heavy to manage.
others.B: Direct Connect gateways connect on-premises networks to VPCs; they do not route traffic between VPCs.
others.D: PrivateLink exposes specific services one way through endpoints, not full network connectivity between VPCs.

tip: Many VPCs, transitive routing = Transit Gateway (peer across Regions).

why: Amazon EFS Standard (Regional) stores data across multiple AZs and gives a mount target in each AZ. ECS tasks can mount it natively, and AWS Backup can copy EFS backups to another Region on a schedule that meets an 8-hour RPO.

others.A: FSx for Windows Multi-AZ uses only two AZs (preferred and standby subnets), not a mount target in every AZ, and it is SMB-oriented.
others.B: FSx for NetApp ONTAP Multi-AZ also spans only two AZs and does not give a mount target in each AZ.
others.D: FSx for OpenZFS is a single-AZ or two-AZ deployment, not a mount target per AZ.

tip: Mount target in every AZ, NFS for containers = EFS.

why: IAM groups get permissions by attaching IAM policies. A least-privilege customer managed policy attached to each department group automatically applies to all current and new users added to it, which is the most secure and scalable approach.

others.A: SCPs set the maximum permissions for accounts in Organizations; they grant nothing to users.
others.B: Roles cannot be attached to groups; roles are assumed, not attached.
others.D: Permissions boundaries limit maximum permissions but grant nothing on their own, and associating roles does not grant permissions to group users.

others.C: Presumably uses the wrong action or resource ARN, so deletion would still fail.
