why: S3 Object Lock, which requires versioning and is easiest to enable on a new bucket, set with a retention period up to the designated date prevents changes or deletions. A static website plus a bucket policy that allows public s3:GetObject makes the files publicly readable.

others.A: IAM permissions apply only to AWS principals, not anonymous public users, and nothing stops bucket owners from changing the files.
others.C: Lambda-based restore is reactive; files can still be changed or deleted, briefly exposing wrong content.
others.D: Object Lock cannot be applied by selecting a folder in an existing bucket, and IAM permissions do not give anonymous public read access.

why: Defining the validated infrastructure (Auto Scaling group, ALB, RDS across two AZs) as an AWS CloudFormation template gives repeatable infrastructure as code. You can deploy identical development and production stacks immediately and automatically.

others.A: Systems Manager handles operations on existing resources, not replicating whole infrastructure stacks.
others.C: AWS Config records and evaluates resource configurations; it cannot deploy infrastructure.
others.D: Elastic Beanstalk cannot reference a manually built prototype and turn it into new environments automatically.

tip: Repeatable environments = CloudFormation (IaC).

why: A VPC endpoint for S3 (a gateway endpoint, or an interface endpoint through PrivateLink) sends EC2 to S3 traffic over the AWS private network instead of the public internet. Bucket policies can then require aws:SourceVpce.

others.A: KMS encrypts data but does not change the network path the traffic takes.
others.C: A private subnet still reaches S3's public endpoints through a NAT gateway and the internet unless a VPC endpoint is used.
others.D: A virtual private gateway is for VPN connections to on-premises networks, not for reaching S3.

why: With write-through caching, the application writes to the cache at the same moment it writes to the database. The cache therefore always has current data that matches the database, which is exactly what the requirement asks for.

others.A: Lazy loading fills the cache only on a cache miss, so cached data can be stale or missing after database writes.
others.C: Adding a TTL only limits how long stale data lives; it does not keep the cache in sync on every write.
others.D: AWS AppConfig manages application configuration and feature flags, not a database caching strategy.

tip: Always consistent = write-through; only cache what is read = lazy loading; combine with TTL for best results.

why: 100 GB over 100 Mbps takes only a few hours, so an online transfer is fine. AWS DataSync is a managed service that encrypts data in transit with TLS, runs parallel transfers, checks integrity and retries automatically, giving a secure migration with little operational overhead.

others.A: aws s3 sync also uses HTTPS and is a reasonable approach, but you must run and monitor it yourself, with no built-in verification, scheduling or reporting.
others.C: Snowball needs days of ordering and shipping, which is slower and more effort for just 100 GB.
others.D: An IPsec VPN is unnecessary because S3 endpoints already use HTTPS, and setting one up adds overhead.

tip: Snowball is worth it only when the online transfer would take more than about a week.

why: ECS on Fargate supports Windows containers, and an EventBridge-driven ECS scheduled task launches the job every 10 minutes. You pay only while each task runs for 1 to 3 minutes, with no servers to manage, which makes it the most cost-effective choice.

others.A: Lambda container images must be Linux-based, so a Windows container cannot run on Lambda.
others.B: AWS Batch on Fargate does not support Windows containers.
others.D: Windows Task Scheduler inside a standalone task would require the task to run all the time, so you pay for idle time.

why: AWS Organizations with all features enabled creates and centrally governs the new business-unit accounts. IAM Identity Center, set up in the organization and connected to the corporate directory (Active Directory through Directory Service, or an external IdP via SAML/SCIM), gives single sign-on to every account.

others.B: Cognito identity pools are for app end users, not workforce access to AWS accounts.
others.C: SCPs limit permissions but do not authenticate anyone, and Identity Center is not added to Directory Service.
others.D: Organizations has no authentication mechanism of its own that can be pointed at Directory Service.

tip: Workforce SSO across many accounts = Organizations + IAM Identity Center + corporate IdP.

why: S3 Glacier storage is very cheap for rarely accessed archives. Expedited retrievals usually return data within 1 to 5 minutes, which meets the 5-minute limit on the rare occasions files are needed.

others.B: Standard Glacier retrievals take 3 to 5 hours, far beyond 5 minutes.
others.C: Standard-IA gives instant access but costs much more to store than Glacier for archives that are rarely read.
others.D: One Zone-IA costs more to store than Glacier and keeps data in only one AZ.

tip: Glacier Flexible Retrieval: Expedited 1-5 min, Standard 3-5 h, Bulk 5-12 h. Glacier Instant Retrieval is an alternative with millisecond access.

why: S3 hosts the static site cheaply with no servers. ECS on Fargate runs the containers serverlessly with simpler deployment than EKS, and RDS provides a managed relational database, which reduces both operational work and cost.

others.B: CloudFront is a CDN, not a place to store files on its own, and ECS on EC2 means managing container instances.
others.C: EKS adds Kubernetes complexity and a per-cluster control plane fee compared with ECS.
others.D: Hosting static content on EC2 Reserved Instances and running EKS on EC2 is the most operationally heavy option.

tip: Simplest container compute = ECS on Fargate.

why: Amazon EFS is an elastic NFS file system with no minimum size that scales automatically. Mount targets in multiple AZs make it highly available, and Linux instances in AWS and on premises (over the Site-to-Site VPN) can mount it with native NFS.

others.A: FSx deployments have minimum storage capacities, and the option does not name an FSx type with native Linux NFS access.
others.B: EBS Multi-Attach volumes are block storage limited to one AZ and cannot be mounted from on premises.
others.D: A single mount target puts the file system in one AZ, so it is not highly available.

why: Service control policies apply to every principal in member accounts, including the root user. An SCP on the root OU that denies billing actions (for example aws-portal:*, billing:* or ce:*) blocks access to billing information in all member accounts.

others.A: Granting the finance team billing access does nothing to restrict others.
others.B: Identity-based policies cannot be attached to the root user, so they cannot restrict it.
others.D: Moving to consolidated billing only would remove SCPs, the very feature that is needed.

tip: Restrict the root user of member accounts = SCP.

why: SNS subscriptions can have a dead-letter queue, an SQS queue that receives messages SNS could not deliver after its retries. Setting the SQS retention period to its 14-day maximum keeps failed order messages for analysis with only configuration changes.

others.A: SNS dead-letter queues must be SQS queues; Kinesis Data Streams cannot be one.
others.B: Putting SQS in front of SNS does not capture messages that fail to reach the HTTPS endpoint after SNS.
others.D: DynamoDB cannot be an SNS dead-letter queue target.

tip: SQS retention: 4 days by default, 1 minute to 14 days configurable.

why: DynamoDB export to S3 needs point-in-time recovery (continuous backups) enabled. It reads from the PITR backup data, not the live table, so it uses no read capacity and does not affect availability, and it needs no code.

others.A: A Hive job on EMR means building and running a cluster, and scanning the table uses RCUs.
others.C: Streams plus Lambda requires custom code and only captures changes, not a full backup of existing data.
others.D: A Lambda export function requires code, and scanning tables uses RCUs.

why: SQS standard queues guarantee at-least-once delivery and cost less than FIFO queues. SSE-KMS encrypts the sensitive card data, and Lambda's execution role needs kms:Decrypt to read the encrypted messages through the event source mapping.

others.B: FIFO queues cost more and give exactly-once processing, which is not needed, and SSE-SQS gives less key control for bank data.
others.C: FIFO queues are more expensive than needed for at-least-once processing.
others.D: Lambda needs kms:Decrypt on its execution role, not an invocation permission on the key.

tip: At least once = SQS standard; exactly once in order = FIFO.

why: Grouping the development accounts into an OU and attaching an SCP that denies ec2:RunInstances unless ec2:InstanceType matches an allowed list blocks oversized instances centrally. It needs no development effort.

others.A: Systems Manager templates do not stop staff from launching instances directly, and building them takes development work.
others.C: EventBridge plus Lambda reacts after creation and needs custom code.
others.D: Service Catalog products take setup work and still need extra IAM restrictions to stop direct launches.

why: Amazon Transcribe converts the call recordings to text (with automatic language identification). Amazon Translate translates that text into English. Amazon Comprehend performs sentiment analysis to produce the reports. All three are fully managed AI services, so no ML models need maintaining.

others.A: Amazon Comprehend analyzes text; it does not translate audio.
others.B: Amazon Lex builds conversational chatbots and does not perform sentiment analysis reporting.
others.C: Amazon Polly converts text to speech, the opposite of what is needed.

tip: Speech to text = Transcribe; text to speech = Polly; translation = Translate; sentiment = Comprehend.

why: The policy, which is not shown, allows ec2:TerminateInstances only when aws:SourceIp is in 192.0.2.0/24 or 203.0.113.0/24. The administrator's CLI request comes from another IP, so the condition fails and the implicit deny returns 403.

others.A: EC2 instances do not support resource-based policies.
others.B: Identity-based policies attached to roles do not specify a Principal element.
others.C: The Action field does include the termination action; the problem is the IP condition.

tip: aws:SourceIp checks the caller's public IP; it is not evaluated for calls made through VPC endpoints.

why: Amazon Macie uses managed data identifiers to discover sensitive data in S3, such as passport numbers, credit card numbers and other PII. A sensitive data discovery job on the data lake bucket produces findings that show where this data is.

others.A: Audit Manager collects evidence for compliance frameworks but does not scan S3 object contents for PII.
others.B: S3 Inventory lists object metadata, not object contents.
others.D: S3 Select queries one object at a time with SQL; it has no PII detection.

tip: Find PII in S3 = Macie.

why: An S3 File Gateway replaces the NFS storage with NFS shares backed by S3 and caches frequently used data locally. A Volume Gateway in cached mode replaces the block storage with iSCSI volumes backed by AWS, with local caching. Neither requires re-architecting the applications.

others.A: S3 cannot be mounted natively as a file system on servers, and doing so with third-party tools gives no local caching.
others.C: Snowball Edge is for data transfer or edge computing, not ongoing hybrid storage expansion.
others.E: Mounting EFS from on premises gives no local caching and adds WAN latency.

tip: Storage Gateway types: S3 File (NFS/SMB to S3), FSx File (SMB), Volume (iSCSI block), Tape (VTL).

why: An S3 gateway VPC endpoint is free and sends S3 traffic from the private subnet over the AWS network through a route table entry. That removes NAT gateway hourly and per-GB processing charges for this heavy traffic, so it is the most cost-effective fix.

others.A: A NAT instance still has instance and management costs, and S3 traffic still leaves through public endpoints.
others.B: A NAT instance must sit in a public subnet, and routing the public subnet through it makes no sense.
others.D: A second NAT gateway adds more hourly and data processing charges.

tip: NAT gateway costs for S3 or DynamoDB traffic = add gateway endpoints.

why: S3 Lifecycle noncurrent version expiration can keep a set number of newer noncurrent versions (NewerNoncurrentVersions) and permanently delete older ones automatically. That retains the latest versions and cuts storage cost with no code to run.

others.B: A custom Lambda function to list and delete versions must be built, scheduled and maintained.
others.C: Batch Operations jobs need manifests and repeated manual runs, and they have no built-in way to keep N versions.
others.D: Versioning cannot be turned off once enabled, only suspended, and suspending it would break the version-based design.

tip: Keep the last N versions = lifecycle rule with NewerNoncurrentVersions.

why: With under 10 percent of 1 Gbps in use (under 100 Mbps), a 200 Mbps hosted connection from a Direct Connect Partner costs much less. It is still a private, dedicated-capacity link, so security is not compromised.

others.A: A new 1 Gbps connection keeps the same oversized capacity, and sharing it with another account raises security concerns.
others.B: Speeds below 1 Gbps (like 200 Mbps) are available only as hosted connections through Partners, not ordered as dedicated connections in the console.
others.C: Ordering another 1 Gbps connection does not lower the cost of unused bandwidth.

tip: Dedicated connections: 1, 10, 100 Gbps. Sub-1 Gbps speeds = hosted connection through a Partner.

why: AWS DataSync can copy SMB data straight into FSx for Windows File Server and preserves NTFS permissions (ACLs), timestamps and metadata. You can run DataSync agents on premises, or on a Snowcone device that runs the DataSync agent, and transfer to FSx online.

others.B: Copying to S3 with the CLI loses Windows ACLs, so permissions cannot be restored in FSx.
others.C: AWS does not offer an import service for raw drives shipped to it, and S3 would not keep NTFS permissions.
others.E: Copying to Snowball with the AWS CLI puts the files in S3 as objects and loses the NTFS ACLs.

tip: Keep Windows ACLs when moving to FSx = DataSync (SMB to FSx).

why: Kinesis Data Firehose is a fully managed ingestion service that delivers directly to S3, with no shards to manage. Kinesis Data Analytics (now Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink) can analyze the stream in real time, which together gives the most operational efficiency.

others.A: Kinesis Data Streams requires managing shards, and writing to S3 requires extra code or a Firehose delivery stream.
others.B: AWS Glue is an ETL service for batch or streaming jobs, not a simple real-time ingestion endpoint.
others.D: API Gateway plus Lambda means custom code for ingestion, analysis and writing to S3.

tip: Stream into S3 with no management = Firehose; real-time SQL or Flink = Managed Service for Apache Flink.

why: Moving images to Amazon EFS gives a shared file system that every instance can mount. An AMI-based Auto Scaling group with at least two instances behind an ALB removes the single instance as a point of failure. CloudFront caches images and pages at the edge for better performance.

others.A: S3 cannot be natively mounted as a file system on EC2 for a CMS that expects file storage.
others.B: An NFS share served from one primary instance is still a single point of failure.
others.D: Global Accelerator speeds up TCP/UDP routing but does not cache content, so CloudFront suits a website better.

why: The secure cross-account pattern has each customer create an IAM role with read-only EC2 and CloudWatch permissions and a trust policy for the company's account, ideally with an external ID. The company assumes the role with STS to get temporary credentials, so no long-term secrets are shared.

others.B: A token vending machine cannot mint credentials in customer accounts without access to them first, and it is complex custom infrastructure.
others.C: Storing customers' long-term IAM user access keys is risky even when encrypted.
others.D: Cognito is for app end-user identity, not cross-account access to AWS APIs, and storing passwords is insecure.

tip: Third-party cross-account access = IAM role + external ID (guards against the confused deputy problem).

why: The keyed option's text is missing. The intended answer is to create a transit gateway in the networking account and share it with the other accounts through AWS Resource Access Manager, then attach each VPC. One hub with transitive routing is the most operationally efficient way to connect hundreds of accounts' VPCs.

others.A: A full mesh of VPC peering across hundreds of VPCs is impossible to manage and has per-VPC peering limits.
others.B: Sending private traffic over the internet through NAT and internet gateways is insecure and does not connect VPCs privately.
others.D: VPN gateways in each VPC mean many VPN tunnels to manage and limited bandwidth.

tip: Share a transit gateway across accounts with AWS RAM.
flag: Option C's text is missing in the source data; the intended correct option is a transit gateway in the networking account shared via AWS RAM with VPC attachments.

why: The batch jobs tolerate interruption, since a failed job is retried on another instance, and they run only 6 hours a night. Spot Instances give up to 90 percent savings for this fault-tolerant, part-time workload, and using them in the Auto Scaling group's launch template is the cheapest option.

others.A: A Savings Plan commits to spending 24 hours a day, but the instances run only 6 hours a day.
others.B: A Reserved Instance bills around the clock for capacity used only a quarter of the day.
others.D: Larger On-Demand instances cost more and add no savings.

tip: Interruptible and retryable = Spot.

why: Presigned URLs let browsers upload directly to S3 using temporary, limited permissions. S3 scales automatically to very high request rates, and the application servers are taken out of the upload data path, which gives the most scalability during event spikes.

others.A: Routing uploads through application servers makes them a bottleneck that must scale with the upload traffic.
others.B: Storage Gateway is for hybrid access from on premises, and browsers cannot upload to it directly.
others.D: Browsers cannot write to an EFS file system directly; it must be mounted by compute resources.

why: The keyed option, which is truncated, converts the application to DynamoDB, presumably with global tables. Global tables replicate between Regions in typically under 1 second and give each Regional deployment a local table, which serves global users with low-latency updates.

others.B: Aurora cross-Region replicas or an Aurora Global Database keep a single writer with sub-second replication, which arguably fits the single-primary requirement, but the key prefers DynamoDB.
others.C: RDS for MySQL cross-Region read replicas replicate asynchronously with more lag and no managed global failover.
others.D: Separate Aurora Serverless databases synchronized by Lambda is a fragile custom design that cannot guarantee global consistency.

tip: Single writer + sub-second cross-Region replication = Aurora Global Database; multi-active = DynamoDB global tables.
flag: The requirement for a single primary database with sub-1-second replication matches Aurora Global Database (option B) better than DynamoDB global tables, which are multi-active; votes are split about 52/48.

why: Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager EBS-backed AMI policies can create AMIs by tag on a schedule (twice a day) and copy them to us-west-2 automatically. AWS Backup plans by tag can likewise back up twice daily with a cross-Region copy to a vault in us-west-2. Both meet the 24-hour RPO with full automation.

others.A: Copying images on demand is manual, so DR copies are not automated.
others.C: A custom Lambda function to copy backups is unnecessary because AWS Backup has built-in cross-Region copy rules.
others.E: Copying on demand to us-west-2 is manual and goes against the automation requirement.

why: Network ACLs support explicit deny rules. Adding inbound deny rules for the few attacking IP addresses on the web tier (ALB) subnets drops their traffic before it reaches the load balancer, which immediately eases the performance problem.

others.A: Security groups do not support deny rules.
others.C: Security groups cannot deny, and the app tier only sees traffic from the ALB, not the client IPs.
others.D: The application tier subnets receive traffic from the ALB's private IPs, so denying client IPs there has no effect.

tip: Block specific IPs fast = NACL deny (or WAF IP set); security groups cannot deny.

why: The keyed option is a garbled fragment. The intended answer sets up an inter-Region VPC peering connection between the eu-west-1 and ap-southeast-2 VPCs, updates both route tables, and adds a database security group rule allowing the application servers. Inter-Region peering traffic is encrypted and stays on the AWS backbone.

others.A: This is a truncated peering option without route table and security group configuration.
others.B: This is also a truncated peering option missing the required routing and security group steps.
others.D: A transit gateway attaches to VPCs in its own Region only; cross-Region connectivity needs a transit gateway in each Region with peering, and security groups cannot reference SG IDs across Regions.

tip: Security group references to peer SGs work only within the same Region; use CIDR blocks for inter-Region peering.
flag: Option C's text is a garbled fragment (about transit gateway peering) in the source data; the intended correct option is inter-Region VPC peering with route tables and an SG rule allowing the app servers' CIDR.

why: Aurora On-Demand, which here means Aurora Serverless for PostgreSQL, scales compute with use and can scale to zero or pause when idle, so you pay mostly for the half-day each environment is actually used. That makes it the most cost-effective option for intermittent development databases.

others.A: Provisioned Aurora instances bill every hour whether or not developers use them.
others.B: RDS Single-AZ instances also bill continuously unless someone stops and starts them by hand.
others.D: S3 Select is not a PostgreSQL database and cannot support the schema.

tip: Intermittent or dev/test relational workloads = Aurora Serverless v2 (supports auto-pause to zero).

why: AWS Backup plans can select resources by tag. Using AWS Config to find untagged resources and then tagging them programmatically brings every resource into the tag-based backup plan, so all resources are backed up with little ongoing effort.

others.B: Whether a resource is running has nothing to do with backup coverage, and resources are not added to vaults directly.
others.C: Manual reviews by every account owner have high overhead and are error-prone.
others.D: Amazon Inspector scans for vulnerabilities and does not identify resources for backup.
